families.s: HSE display-screen-equipment workstation and user-protection guidance
families.t: DSE-user identification, workstation assessment, posture, breaks, eyesight, training and home or hybrid use
f: Employers must protect workers from health risks arising from daily display-screen-equipment use.
The DSE Regulations apply to users working with display screens daily for continuous periods of an hour or more.
Employers must assess DSE workstations and reduce identified risks.
DSE work should be interrupted by breaks or changes of activity.
Employers must arrange an eyesight test for a DSE user who requests one.
Employers must provide special corrective appliances when they are required only for DSE work.
DSE users must receive information and training covering posture, adjustment, glare, breaks, assessments and reporting problems.
The HSE DSE checklist reviews keyboards, pointing devices, screens, software, furniture and the work environment.
families.g: DSE risk depends on actual duration and pattern of use, workstation geometry, posture, equipment, lighting, task demands, individual needs and whether work occurs at home, on site or across both.

families.s: HSE work-related-stress risk-assessment and Management Standards guidance
families.t: prevention, risk assessment, worker consultation and management of demands, control, support, relationships, role and change
f: Employers must assess and act on risks to workers from work-related stress.
HSE's Management Standards provide a step-by-step risk-assessment approach focused on underlying causes and prevention.
The six Management Standards areas are demands, control, support, relationships, role and change.
Demands include workload, work patterns and the work environment and should be achievable within agreed working hours.
Control includes workers having appropriate influence over pace, breaks, work patterns and how they use their skills.
Support includes access to information, resources, constructive feedback and help from managers and colleagues.
Relationships controls should promote positive behaviour, prevent conflict and provide ways to report unacceptable behaviour.
Role and change arrangements should clarify responsibilities, avoid conflicting requirements and communicate and consult on organisational change.
families.g: Stress risk depends on work design and organisation, worker characteristics and experience, duration, support, workplace relationships, role clarity, change and the effectiveness of collective and individual controls.

families.s: HSE work-related violence and aggression prevention guidance
families.t: legal duties, hazard identification, risk assessment, physical and organisational controls, incident reporting and worker support
f: Work-related violence includes abuse, threats and assaults arising from work, including verbal and online abuse.
Employers must protect workers from work-related violence so far as reasonably practicable.
Risk assessments must include the risk of work-related violence and aggression.
Employers should consult workers and representatives when identifying violence hazards and practical controls.
A written risk assessment alone does not reduce violence; the resulting actions and controls must be implemented.
Where violence cannot be eliminated, employers should use a combination of controls rather than relying on a single measure.
Arrangements should address prevention, training, reporting, learning from incidents and support after physical or psychological harm.
Specified injuries, dangerous occurrences or occupational diseases arising from violent incidents may be reportable under RIDDOR.
families.g: Violence risk depends on sector and task, public contact, lone work, time and location, authority over customers, valuables, alcohol or drugs, staffing, workplace design, communications and incident history.

families.s: HSE lone-worker risk-management, supervision and monitoring guidance
families.t: risk assessment, communication, supervision, competence, violence, medical suitability, high-risk work and emergency response
f: Employers must manage health and safety risks before people work alone, including contractors and relevant self-employed workers.
Lone workers face greater consequences when no one is nearby to provide help or support.
Employers must train, supervise and monitor lone workers, keep in contact and respond to incidents.
Risk assessment should consider violence, stress, mental health, medical suitability and isolated or rural workplaces.
Some high-risk activities require another person, including specified confined-space, live-electrical, diving, explosives-vehicle and fumigation work.
Lone work may increase vulnerability to violence because nearby support is unavailable.
Training should define limits, prepare workers for unexpected situations and explain when they must seek advice.
The level of supervision and monitoring should increase with the level of risk.
families.g: Lone-working risk depends on the task, location, communication reliability, foreseeable emergencies, worker competence and health, violence exposure, supervision, travel and response time.

families.s: HSE workplace first-aid needs, personnel, equipment and training guidance
families.t: needs assessment, first-aid kits, appointed persons, trained first-aiders, information, competence and coverage
f: Employers must ensure employees receive immediate help if they are injured or taken ill at work.
Every workplace must have a suitably stocked first-aid kit.
Every workplace must appoint a person or people to take charge of first-aid arrangements.
Employees must be given information about the workplace first-aid arrangements.
First-aid provision should be based on a first-aid needs assessment reflecting the workplace circumstances.
A first-aider must have training and a valid certificate appropriate to the circumstances.
HSE's optional framework includes appointed person, emergency first aid at work, first aid at work and additional training.
Where a first-aider is unnecessary, an appointed person can manage equipment and facilities and call emergency services.
families.g: First-aid needs depend on hazards, workforce size and distribution, shift and absence cover, remoteness, accident history, non-employees, travel and access to emergency medical services.

families.s: HSE manual-handling avoidance, assessment and risk-reduction guidance
families.t: avoidance, task-load-individual-environment assessment, mechanical aids, workplace design, training and technique
f: Manual handling includes lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling, carrying or moving an object, person or animal by bodily force.
Employers must avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable.
Unavoidable hazardous manual handling must be assessed for injury risk.
The remaining risk must be reduced to as low as reasonably practicable.
The law does not set a single safe weight limit for manual handling.
Mechanical assistance, task changes, smaller loads and improved workplace layout can reduce risk.
Good handling technique supplements rather than replaces elimination, lifting aids and task or workplace improvements.
Assessment should account for the task, load, individual capability and working environment.
families.g: Manual-handling risk depends on load weight and stability, frequency and distance, posture and reach, grip, pace, environment, individual capability, team handling and available mechanical aids.

families.s: HSE occupational-noise assessment, control and hearing-protection guidance
families.t: action and limit values, source control, hearing protection, zones, training, maintenance and audiometric surveillance
f: Employers must assess occupational-noise risks, reduce exposure, provide information and training and arrange health surveillance where required.
The lower daily or weekly exposure action value is 80 dB(A) and the upper value is 85 dB(A).
The daily or weekly exposure limit value is 87 dB(A), taking hearing protection into account.
Peak lower, upper and limit values are 135, 137 and 140 dB(C), respectively.
Hearing protectors are required and their proper use enforced above the upper exposure action value.
Mandatory hearing-protection zones should be identified and marked where required.
Protectors that reduce sound at the ear below about 70 dB should be avoided because overprotection can impair communication and warning detection.
Engineering and organisational noise control should be planned before relying on hearing protection.
families.g: Noise risk depends on level, peak pressure, duration, frequency content, number of sources, room acoustics, equipment condition, worker mobility, protector fit and the reliability of technical controls.

families.s: HSE hand-arm-vibration exposure-control and health-surveillance guidance
families.t: tool selection, exposure assessment, maintenance, work scheduling, symptoms, action values and health surveillance
f: Hand-arm vibration can arise from hand-held tools, hand-guided equipment and materials held against powered machinery.
Regular exposure can damage blood vessels, nerves, muscles and joints in the hands and arms.
Hand-arm vibration syndrome can cause tingling, numbness, reduced grip and vibration white finger.
Employers must assess and control hand-arm-vibration exposure under the Control of Vibration at Work Regulations.
Control measures include reducing exposure duration, selecting lower-vibration equipment and maintaining tools correctly.
Powered grinders, sanders, impact tools and air chisels can create significant hand-arm-vibration exposure.
Workers should be trained in safe tool use and instructed to report pain, numbness or tingling promptly.
Health surveillance is required where the risk assessment shows workers remain at risk from HAV.
families.g: HAV risk depends on vibration magnitude, trigger time, tool and consumable condition, grip and feed force, temperature, maintenance, work pattern, individual susceptibility and control effectiveness.
